---
title: "Lights Out in Afghanistan"
subtitle: "Effects of the 2021 Taliban Takeover"
author:
  - name: Camron Ibrahimi
    email: IbrahimiC@cardiff.ac.uk
date: today
abstract: |
  After the Taliban took Kabul in August 2021, Afghanistan lost most foreign
  aid, access to its central bank reserves and its links to the international
  banking system. The economic consequences were measured using satellite
  nighttime lights from NASA's Black Marble monthly product for 2018–2023.
  Afghanistan was compared with six control countries in South and Central Asia and also
  the Philippines in a difference-in-differences regression analysis. Afghanistan's lit
  radiance falls by about 52% relative to the comparison countries and the
  decline persists for at least two years. The pre-takeover trend is close to flat
  and the result holds across radiance thresholds and sample restrictions.
  A permutation test finds that no comparison country shows a larger decline.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(knitr)

pct <- function(b) round(100 * (exp(b) - 1))   # log points -> % change
r2  <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)

b_main   <- coef(did)[["treated:post"]]
se_main  <- se(summary(did, vcov = ~country))[["treated:post"]]
n_ctry   <- length(unique(panel$country))
n_months <- length(unique(panel$month))
n_drop   <- nrow(panel_all) - nrow(panel)

es_coef  <- coef(es)            # yearly event-study estimates
names(es_coef) <- sub(".*::(-?[0-9]+):.*", "\\1", names(es_coef))

afg_rank <- rank(effects)[["Afghanistan"]]   # 1 = biggest drop of all countries

placebo_time <- summary(
  feols(log_lights ~ treated:post | country^calendar_month + month,
        data = fake_time),
  vcov = ~country
)
```

# Introduction

On 15 August 2021, Taliban forces entered Kabul and the internationally
recognised government (Islamic Republic of Afghanistan) collapsed.
This was the same government that was previously backed, financed and protected by the United States and its
NATO allies. The economic shock that followed was not mainly
a result of fighting, but of the suspension of donor grants, which had previously funded most public
spending. Afghanistan's central bank lost access to its
reserves held abroad. Correspondent banks cut ties with the Afghan
financial system as a result. This disrupted trade payments in particular and the remittances many
households depended on
[@worldbank2022adu].

Measuring what followed shortly after is hard, because official statistics largely
stopped. This note uses an outcome that does not depend on the Afghan state:
light visible from space at night. Nighttime lights track economic activity
well where national accounts may be weak or simply missing
[@henderson2012; @chen2011].

Afghanistan's lights were compared with those of `r n_ctry - 1` comparison
countries before and after the takeover. The main estimate is a
**`r abs(pct(b_main))`%** decline in lit radiance relative to the comparison
group. The fall began with the Taliban offensive in mid-2021 and was yet to
reverse by the end of 2023.

# Data {#sec-data}

**Nighttime lights.** NASA's Black Marble VNP46A3 monthly product
[@roman2018], which corrects VIIRS radiance for moonlight, atmosphere and
cloud cover. The panel covers `r n_months` months (January 2018 to December
2023) for `r n_ctry` countries. National boundaries come from Natural Earth.

**Measuring "lights".** Most of Afghanistan is dark, so averages over all
pixels are dominated by noise. The product records radiance below 0.5 nW as
zero and a large number of faint background pixels just above that floor
made the national mean jump in 2023, while brighter, clearly lit areas remained constant.
The outcome is therefore the **log of total radiance from pixels brighter than 2 nW**, which isolates
settled, lit areas. Thresholds of 1 nW and 5 nW
give similar results (@sec-robust).

**Coverage.** Some months have many missing pixels, mainly winter months in
Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan where snow and cloud block the satellite.
Country-months where less than 80% of pixels are valid were dropped. This removes
`r n_drop` of `r nrow(panel_all)` observations. Keeping them changes little.

**Comparison countries.** Bangladesh, Kyrgyzstan, Nepal, Pakistan, the
Philippines, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. These are lower- and middle-income
countries in or near the region that also rely on remittances.

```{r}
include_graphics("../figures/indexed_lights.png")
```

# Empirical strategy

The estimated difference-in-differences model is

$$
\log L_{ct} = \alpha_{c,m(t)} + \lambda_t + \beta \,(\text{Afghanistan}_c \times \text{Post}_t) + \varepsilon_{ct}
$$

where $L_{ct}$ is lit radiance in country $c$ and month $t$, and
$\text{Post}_t$ equals one from August 2021. The country-by-calendar-month
effects $\alpha_{c,m(t)}$ absorb each country's own seasonal pattern (for
example festival lighting or winter heating). The month effects
$\lambda_t$ absorb shocks common to all countries, such as COVID-19. $\beta$
measures how much Afghanistan's lights changed after the takeover beyond
the change in the comparison countries.

To check the timing, an event study was estimated. This replaced
$\text{Post}_t$ with indicators for each year relative to the takeover,
where each year runs from August to July. The reference year is
August 2019 to July 2020, well before the 2021 offensive.

**Inference.** With one treated country and `r n_ctry - 1` controls,
conventional clustered standard errors are unreliable
[@conley2011; @cameron2008]. The main evidence is a
permutation test in the spirit of @abadie2010: each comparison country is
analysed in turn as if it had been "treated", to see how
unusual Afghanistan's estimate truly is.

# Results

```{r}
#| label: tbl-main
#| tbl-cap: "Difference-in-differences estimates. Standard errors clustered by country in parentheses."
# Each row is one model. robust_models is defined here so the table and the
# text use exactly the same estimates.
spec <- log_lights ~ treated:post | country^calendar_month + month
robust_models <- list(
  "Main (> 2 nW)"           = did,
  "> 1 nW"                  = feols(log(lit_sum_1) ~ treated:post | country^calendar_month + month, panel),
  "> 5 nW"                  = feols(log(lit_sum_5) ~ treated:post | country^calendar_month + month, panel),
  "Drop Pakistan"           = feols(spec, filter(panel, country != "Pakistan")),
  "Drop Nepal"              = feols(spec, filter(panel, country != "Nepal")),
  "Drop Aug 2021"           = feols(spec, filter(panel, month != "2021-08")),
  "Drop May–Jul 2021"       = feols(spec, filter(panel, !month %in% c("2021-05", "2021-06", "2021-07"))),
  "No coverage filter"      = feols(spec, panel_all)
)

# Pull estimate, SE and N out of each model into one data frame
rows <- lapply(robust_models, function(m) {
  s <- summary(m, vcov = ~country)
  b <- coef(s)[["treated:post"]]
  data.frame(
    Estimate   = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", b, se(s)[["treated:post"]]),
    `% change` = paste0(pct(b), "%"),
    N          = nobs(m),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
})
tab <- do.call(rbind, rows)
kable(tab, align = "rrr")
```

@tbl-main reports the estimates. In the main specification, Afghanistan's
lit radiance falls by `r r2(abs(b_main))` log points (standard error
`r r2(se_main)`) relative to the comparison countries, a decline of about
**`r abs(pct(b_main))`%**. @fig-index shows where this comes from:
Afghanistan tracks the other countries until mid-2021, then drops and stays
down while the comparison countries recover from COVID-19.

```{r}
#| label: fig-es
#| fig-cap: "Event study: Afghanistan minus comparison countries, by year relative to the takeover (August–July years). Reference year −2 (Aug 2019–Jul 2020). Bars are 95% confidence intervals clustered by country."
include_graphics("../figures/event_study.png")
```

@fig-es shows the timing. The two earliest years lie slightly above zero
(`r r2(es_coef[["-4"]])` and `r r2(es_coef[["-3"]])`), and year −1, which
includes the start of the Taliban offensive, is `r r2(es_coef[["-1"]])`.
After the takeover the estimates drop to between `r r2(min(es_coef[c("0","1","2")]))`
and `r r2(max(es_coef[c("0","1","2")]))` and stay there for all three post-takeover
years (the last observed only through December 2023). The effect does not seem to fade.

# Inference and robustness {#sec-robust}

**Permutation test.** When "treatment" is re-assigned to each country in turn,
Afghanistan's estimate ranks `r afg_rank` of `r n_ctry`: no comparison
country shows a larger decline. The one-sided permutation p-value is
`r sprintf("%.3f", mean(effects <= effects[["Afghanistan"]]))`. This is the smallest
value possible with `r n_ctry` countries, so it is the strongest evidence
this test can give. It should be read as "Afghanistan is the most extreme
case in the sample", not simply as significance at conventional levels.

**Placebo in time.** Using only data up to April 2021 and pretending the
takeover happened in August 2019 gives an estimate of `r r2(b_placebo)`
(p = `r r2(p_placebo)`), close to zero, as it should be if nothing
unusual was happening to Afghanistan before 2021.

**Specification checks.** @tbl-main shows that the result holds for
radiance thresholds of 1, 2 and 5 nW, without the coverage filter, and when
dropping the takeover month or the offensive months of May–July 2021. Dropping
Pakistan or Nepal also leaves the estimate largely unchanged.

# Limitations

- **Few countries.** With only one treated country, the inference relies on a
  permutation test with only `r n_ctry` possible outcomes. Clustered
  standard errors with so few clusters can be misleadingly small. The
  "Drop Nepal" row, with an unusually small standard error, is an example.
- **Mild pre-trend.** Afghanistan's lights were drifting slightly down
  relative to the comparison countries before 2021. The drift is small next
  to the post-takeover drop, but it means that part of the estimate could reflect
  an earlier decline.
- **Contaminated controls.** Pakistan borders Afghanistan, trades heavily
  with the country and received refugees after the takeover, so it was affected
  too. Nepal's lights grew unusually fast over the period. Neither country drives
  the result (@tbl-main), but no comparison group can ever be perfect.
- **What lights measure.** Lights capture electricity use and visible
  economic activity, not income directly. Some of the decline may also reflect
  cuts in electricity imports or public lighting, not only lower private
  activity.
- **Mechanisms.** This design measures the combined effect of the takeover.
  It cannot separate the aid cut-off, the banking freeze, the disruption to
  remittances and the changes in governance.

# Conclusion

Satellite data show a large and lasting fall in Afghanistan's economic
activity after August 2021: lit radiance fell by about
`r abs(pct(b_main))`% relative to comparable countries, with no recovery
by the end of 2023. Because the outcome is measured from space, this
estimate does not depend on official statistics, which largely stopped
after the takeover. A natural next step would be to use subnational data, comparing
provinces that relied more on aid or remittances before 2021, in order to separate
the channels behind the decline.
